title: Spiritual Warfare: A Bible Study on the Unseen Battle
subtitle: A five-session study on the powers, the armor of God, and the war we can't see.
summary:
This study is for Christians who suspect the New Testament means something real when it says our fight isn't against flesh and blood, and who are tired of choosing between two poor options: the church that finds a demon behind every bush and the church that has quietly stopped believing in the devil at all. Over five sessions it takes up the New Testament's picture of the powers, the armor of God read piece by piece, temptation and the enemy within, the victory Christ won at the cross, and the plain means by which ordinary Christians stand: prayer, Scripture, the gathered church and the Lord's Table. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

C. S. Lewis warned that there are two opposite mistakes we can make about the devils, disbelief and an unhealthy fascination, and that they're pleased by both. This study tries to live between those mistakes. It won't sell you a war story to thrill you, and it won't talk you out of a war the Scriptures plainly describe. The battle is real, the outcome is already decided, and the weapons handed to an ordinary believer are almost embarrassingly plain: a belt, a shield, a book, a prayer, a shared loaf.
audience: Christians, small groups, and anyone unsure what to make of the New Testament's language about the powers

sessions.title: The World Behind the World
sessions.aim: To recover the Bible's picture of the powers, past both the superstition that sees a demon behind every setback and the materialism that says there's nothing behind the world at all, and to see that the New Testament describes a real conflict on a wider front than either error allows.
sessions.summary:
Plenty of thoughtful people say they outgrew the devil about the time they outgrew Santa Claus. No adult believes in a horned figure with a pitchfork, and evil is only the gap between our biology and our ideals. They're right about the pitchfork. But the century that was most sure it had outgrown the devil built death camps with engineers and timetables, and that should make all of us less sure our account of evil is big enough.

Most of us run on one of two accounts, and both are too small. Superstition sees a spirit behind every flat tire and bad mood. Materialism sees nothing behind anything, only atoms and accidents. Each has something right: the first knows there's more to the world than we can see, and the second knows that blaming spirits can become a way to dodge responsibility. Paul cuts both at once. "We do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness" (Ephesians 6:12). The powers are real, personal, and at work through structures that outlive the people who serve them.

keyScripture.why: Paul names the real front of the battle in a way that rules out both the person who sees no war and the person who sees only demons.

discussion.q: Before tonight, which account of evil had more hold on you: the one that sees spiritual attack behind most hard things, or the one that quietly assumes there's nothing behind anything? Where did you pick it up?
discussion.behind: Find out what people assume before you teach anything. Some grew up seeing a demon behind every setback, some absorbed the modern sense that the visible world is all there is, and most carry a mix of both. You're not settling which is right yet, only bringing the assumption into the light. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Ephesians 6:10-12. Paul says "we do not wrestle against flesh and blood" (Ephesians 6:12). When you're in a real conflict, with a person, a habit or an institution, how often do you actually think anything is going on behind the flesh and blood in front of you?
discussion.behind: Many Christians affirm this verse and then live as if every conflict were purely human. You're not trying to make anyone nervous. You're helping the room notice how small its working picture of the world has become.

discussion.q: Some Christians warn that overheated talk about spiritual warfare has made believers fearful and superstitious. What's true in that warning? Have you seen the excess it's worried about?
discussion.behind: Let the room name the harm before the session insists the war is real anyway. Demon-hunting Christianity has frightened people and excused them from responsibility. Grant that fully. Just don't let the right kind of caution turn into unbelief.

discussion.q: Others say the modern West hasn't disproved the powers so much as stopped believing what the apostles believed. What would it cost you to take the New Testament's language about the powers as seriously as it takes itself?
discussion.behind: Now press from the other side. Educated people often translate Paul's plain words into metaphor without noticing they've done it. Ask whether that embarrassment is something we discovered or something we inherited. Keep it curious, not scolding.

discussion.q: Think about the past year. Is there a season you filed under ordinary trouble that might have had more going on beneath it, whether temptation, discouragement or a division that kept outrunning its stated cause?
discussion.behind: Say plainly that not every hard thing is an attack. You're inviting reflection, not drama. If someone's answer gets heavy, thank them and don't rush to interpret it for them.

objections.objection: Talk of demons and dark powers is the kind of prescientific superstition that keeps people from taking responsibility. Blame the devil and you never have to fix the system, the addiction, or yourself.
objections.response: The danger is real, and Scripture shares the concern. A faith that blames a spirit for every failure has found a way never to repent, and the New Testament never lets anyone off the hook by pointing at the devil. When Paul lists "the works of the flesh" (Galatians 5:19), he doesn't say a demon made anyone do them. But naming the powers doesn't remove responsibility in Scripture. It sits beside it. James says each person is tempted "by his own desire" (James 1:14) and, a few chapters later, "Resist the devil" (James 4:7). My sin is mine, and there's also an enemy who works the ground I've left unguarded. Refusing superstition doesn't require materialism. It requires a world with more in it than atoms and less in it than a demon behind every bush.

objections.objection: I'm a rational person. I can't make myself believe in invisible spiritual beings because a first-century text assumes them. That's asking me to switch off my mind.
objections.response: That's a fair thing to say, and nobody here should ask you to be credulous. But it's worth asking whether the closed world is as roomy as it seems. It struggles to account for the excess in human evil, the way cruelty so often goes beyond any useful motive, as though something were being served beyond the calculating self. And the century most confident it had outgrown the devil produced some of the most efficient horrors in history. That doesn't prove Paul right. It does raise the question whether the modern account is large enough for what we see, or whether we called it maturity when we stopped looking. You don't have to switch off your mind to read Paul here. You only have to consider that the map you were handed may have left a country off.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which mistake do you actually live inside, the one that sees an enemy behind every hard thing or the one that has quietly decided nothing is behind anything, and what has it cost you?
sessions.practice: This week, when you hit a real conflict, whether a temptation that seems to come from nowhere or a division at home or church that keeps outrunning its stated cause, pause before you file it entirely under flesh and blood. Don't go hunting for spirits, and don't excuse anyone, yourself included. Just ask whether more might be going on than the surface shows, and pray with that in mind. At the end of the week, write down whether your praying changed when you stopped assuming the visible was the whole field.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made a world with more in it than we can see, and we've shrunk it to what fits our instruments. Some of us have jumped at shadows and blamed a spirit for what our own hands did. Some of us have flattened your world until nothing stood behind it, and called our unbelief maturity. Forgive us both. Open our eyes to the real conflict without making us afraid, and keep us honest about the responsibility that is ours. Teach us to live in the world you actually made, wider than we assumed and safer than we feared, because you hold it. Amen.
reflection: Which of the two mistakes, superstition or materialism, has had the quieter and deeper hold on how I live?
Do I believe Paul when he says my hardest conflicts aren't finally against flesh and blood, or do I affirm it on Sunday and forget it by Monday?
Where have I excused my own sin by blaming an enemy, or dismissed a real enemy by calling everything ordinary trouble?
sessions.teaching:
You've probably met someone who says, a little patiently, that he outgrew the devil about the same time he outgrew Santa Claus. No adult believes in a horned creature with a pitchfork, he says. Evil is the gap between our biology and our ideals, a problem of wiring and upbringing that better conditions will close. He's right about the pitchfork. But it's fair to ask him where the twentieth century came from. It was the century most confident it had outgrown the devil, and it industrialized murder, ran the camps on timetables, and filed the killing under policy. The question isn't whether cartoon devils exist. They don't. The question is whether any of us holds an account of evil large enough for what human beings actually do.

Most of us run on one of two accounts, and both are too small. The first is superstition. A flat tire is an attack, a bad mood is oppression, and the Christian life becomes a nervous scan of the room for the enemy's fingerprints. It gives the devil too much credit, and it lets the sinner place the trouble anywhere but in his own heart. The second is materialism. There's nothing behind the world, only atoms and accidents and an anxious brain, and evil is a word we'll eventually replace with better neuroscience. Few Christians would say that out loud, but many live by it.

I have to be careful here, because I held the second view. I came to faith from atheism, and I know how reasonable the closed world feels from inside, how obvious it seems that the visible is all there is. What I couldn't account for, in the end, was the surplus in human evil, the way cruelty so often outruns any rational motive, as though something were being served beyond the person doing it.

Each account deserves a fair hearing. The sober Christian says that overheated warfare talk has made believers fearful and superstitious, that a deliverance industry has sold fear and excused laziness, and that someone forever binding spirits over a traffic jam may never have done the harder work of repentance. That's true, and I won't add to it. The other side says the modern West hasn't disproved the powers. It has simply stopped believing what the apostles believed and called the change maturity. That's true too. Paul wasn't a peasant afraid of the dark. He was a trained mind writing to sophisticated cities, and he assumed a real enemy without embarrassment.

Then he wrote this: "For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 6:12). That one sentence cuts both errors. It tells the materialist that the visible isn't the whole field. And it tells the superstitious believer that the conflict runs at the level of rulers and authorities, of whole orders of life, not at the level of every stubbed toe. The front is wider and stranger than either of us assumed.

Scripture is consistent about this from the start. Evil first appears in the Bible as a voice, the serpent who was "more crafty than any other beast of the field" (Genesis 3:1), asking a question that makes God's good command sound like a cage. In Job the accuser is real and active, and he's also on a short leash, never acting outside God's permission (Job 1:6-12). Jesus calls him "a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44), which tells us his main weapon isn't spectacle but deception. And Paul says that even "rulers or authorities" were created by Christ (Colossians 1:16). The enemy commands nothing he didn't first receive from the one he rebelled against.

C. S. Lewis put the danger well in the preface to The Screwtape Letters. He wrote that "there are two equal and opposite errors into which our race can fall about the devils. One is to disbelieve in their existence. The other is to believe, and to feel an excessive and unhealthy interest in them." This whole study lives between those errors.

So here is where we'll stand for five weeks. The powers are real. They're personal, and they also work through the institutions and ideologies that outlive the people who serve them, which is part of what Paul means by rulers and authorities. The conflict isn't a metaphor, and it isn't a hobby. It's being fought on ground you walk across every day, and the first thing a soldier has to do is stop pretending he's a civilian.

scriptureStudy.note: "Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made." Evil enters the Bible as a voice, personal and deceptive, asking a question that makes God's good command sound like a cage. The war begins with a lie about God's character, and it still does.

The accuser comes before God and is given a limited leash. The passage holds together what the two errors pull apart: the enemy is real and active, and he is never sovereign or outside God's permission and purpose.

"We do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness." Paul places the real conflict behind the human one, which rules out the materialist who sees only flesh and blood and the believer who fights only visible enemies.

"The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers." The enemy's chief weapon is the quiet blinding that makes the gospel look dull or false, not a dramatic display. Most of his work is done unseen.

"He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth... he is a liar and the father of lies." Jesus names the enemy's native language. Deception is the main front, which is why a Christian who has agreed in advance to see nothing is easily misled.

"Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour." The tone is serious without being frantic. Watchful, not terrified: the posture of someone who knows there's a war and knows who wins it.

"For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities." Even the powers, in their origin, are things Christ made and holds.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The twentieth century produced a serious argument about what Paul's powers actually are, and a group is helped by knowing its shape. The Dutch theologian Hendrik Berkhof, in Christ and the Powers (1953; in English, 1962), argued that Paul's principalities include the structures that govern collective life, such as traditions, ideologies and institutions, which were created good, fell into rebellion, and now bind people rather than serve them. Walter Wink went further in his trilogy, Naming the Powers (1984), Unmasking the Powers (1986) and Engaging the Powers (1992), proposing that the powers are the inner spirit of concrete institutions, so that a corporation or a nation really can have a spirit that turns demonic.

Take the strong form of Wink's case, because it explains something an individual reading misses: evil so often outlives every person involved and takes on a life inside a system no single member intends. Then hear the evangelical critique, made carefully by the New Testament scholar Clinton Arnold in Powers of Darkness (1992), that Wink tends to dissolve the personal enemy into the merely structural, and that Paul plainly means personal spiritual beings and not only the spirit of institutions. You don't have to choose. Scripture holds a personal enemy and the fallen structures he works through. Augustine's The City of God, written between 413 and 426, frames all of history as the conflict of two cities, with evil working through the loves and loyalties of the earthly one. Ask the group which half they tend to lose: the enemy in the heart, or the enemy in the structures.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is an engineer by training, careful and skeptical. He tells you he became a Christian because of the historical case for the resurrection, and he has always treated the language of demons and powers as embarrassing baggage he tolerates for the sake of the rest. He isn't hostile. He's being straight with you, and this session has made him uncomfortable.

Honor his mind before you press it. His skepticism isn't sin, and a group needs someone who won't be stampeded into superstition by a frightening story. Say so. Then notice the shape of his discomfort. He hasn't weighed the New Testament's account of the powers and found it wanting. He let the resurrection in because it has evidence he respects, and he kept the powers outside because they don't fit the world he was raised in.

You might ask him whether the Paul he trusts on the empty tomb is a reliable enough witness to be heard on the conflict he plainly thought he was in. Then leave it with him. Use the case to ask the group which parts of the faith they've accepted on evidence and which parts they've quietly set aside without ever examining them.
