bibliography.title: The Screwtape Letters
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Letters from a senior devil to a junior one (1942). Its preface describes the two opposite errors about the devils that this study tries to avoid. Behind sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: Powers of Darkness: Principalities and Powers in Paul's Letters
bibliography.author: Clinton E. Arnold
bibliography.note: A careful evangelical study of Paul's language of the powers (1992), holding the personal enemy together with the structural and answering readings that turn the powers into institutions only. Supports sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: Christ and the Powers
bibliography.author: Hendrik Berkhof
bibliography.note: A short, influential book (1953; English 1962) arguing that Paul's principalities include the structures of collective life, created good, fallen, and now binding. Background for session 1; it gives less attention to the personal enemy.

bibliography.title: Naming the Powers
bibliography.author: Walter Wink
bibliography.note: The first volume (1984) of a trilogy proposing that the powers are the inner spirit of institutions. Read it for its strong case on structural evil and weigh its tendency to dissolve the personal enemy into the structural.

bibliography.title: Power Encounters: Reclaiming Spiritual Warfare
bibliography.author: David Powlison
bibliography.note: A biblical counselor's critique of the deliverance model (1995), arguing that the New Testament frames the fight mainly in moral terms: truth, repentance, faith and community. Central to sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: Christus Victor
bibliography.author: Gustaf Aulén
bibliography.note: The classic case (English 1931) that the early church saw the cross first as God's triumph over sin, death and the devil. Behind session 4; best read alongside the truth that Christ bore the penalty for sin.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written 413 to 426. Augustine frames history as the conflict of the city of God and the earthly city, with evil working through disordered loves. Long; read selectively.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: About 397 to 400. Book 2's account of stealing pears is a study of a will turned in on itself. Useful for session 3.

bibliography.title: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
bibliography.author: Martin Luther
bibliography.note: The hymn, in print by 1529, that holds together real demonic assault and the plain word that defeats it. Behind sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: Three Crucial Questions about Spiritual Warfare
bibliography.author: Clinton E. Arnold
bibliography.note: A short, readable treatment (1997) of the questions this study raises, between the sober and the charismatic readings. Background for leaders.

bibliography.title: Christ and Time
bibliography.author: Oscar Cullmann
bibliography.note: The 1946 study that pictures the cross as the decisive battle of a war still being fought to its end. Background for session 4.

furtherReading: The Screwtape Letters, C. S. Lewis, for the imaginative picture behind the two mistakes the study tries to avoid.
Powers of Darkness, Clinton Arnold, for a careful study of Paul's language of the powers that keeps both the personal and the structural.
Power Encounters, David Powlison, for the strong case that the fight is mainly one of truth, repentance, faith and community, read alongside the study's insistence on a real enemy.
Christus Victor, Gustaf Aulén, for anyone who wants to stay longer with the cross as a triumph over the powers, held together with Christ's bearing of our sin.
The temptation of Jesus in Matthew 4 and Luke 4, read straight through, to see how the Lord answered a real enemy at the point of a real hunger.

glossary.definition: Paul's language for the spiritual forces behind the Christian's real conflict: "the rulers... the authorities... the cosmic powers over this present darkness" (Ephesians 6:12). Held in this study as personal and also at work through fallen structures and institutions.

The older English word (KJV) for the rulers Paul names. Understood here to include personal spiritual beings and the orders and institutions that were created good, fell, and now bind rather than serve.

C. S. Lewis's description of the two opposite mistakes about the devils: to disbelieve in their existence, and to feel an excessive and unhealthy interest in them. The study tries to stand between them.

The picture in Ephesians 6:10-18 of the Christian life put on like armor: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God. Each piece is already given in Christ and lived out, not recited like a spell.
The word of God (Ephesians 6:17), the one piece of the armor for striking. Jesus used it in the wilderness by answering each lie with a specific written truth.
The command Paul repeats with the armor (Ephesians 6:11, 13, 14). Not conquer or advance, but hold the ground Christ already won, unmoved in the evil day.
In Paul and James, the disordered desires that are really our own, out of which sin is conceived (James 1:14-15; Galatians 5:16-17). The enemy exploits this ground; he doesn't create it.
Usually not the offer of something obviously evil but of something good at the wrong time, on the enemy's terms, aimed at a desire already present, with a lie about God underneath.

Latin for "Christ the Victor": the view, associated with Gustaf Aulén, that the cross is first of all God's triumph over sin, death and the devil. Held here alongside Christ's bearing of the penalty for sin.

glossary.term: The already and the not yet
glossary.definition: The New Testament's frame for the time we live in, between the decisive victory at the cross and its final completion at Christ's return. The enemy is truly defeated and still dangerous.

Resisting the enemy from an outcome already secured at the cross, rather than straining toward one still in doubt. Its opposite, fighting for victory, is the anxious striving of someone who believes the war is undecided.
The plain ways God ordinarily works and Christians stand: the word, prayer, and the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, received in the gathered church.
One of the enemy's roles in Scripture, from Job and Zechariah to Revelation 12:10. His charge is answered not by our self-defense but by the blood of the Lamb.
